passage: At the anganwadi, Deepak Sir poured jaggery chana onto two leaves. 'Irfan, which leaf has more?' Irfan pointed at the bigger heap. 'This one!' 'Let's check.' Irfan counted slowly, touching each chana. 'One, two... seven.' Then the other: 'One... four.' He frowned, then brightened. 'Seven is more! Four is less.' Deepak Sir moved two chana across. Irfan counted again and shouted, 'Now it's five and six!'

qa.q: How many chana did Irfan count on the first leaf?
qa.a: He counted seven chana on the first leaf.

qa.q: Why did Irfan brighten after frowning?
qa.a: He felt pleased when counting confirmed his guess and he understood that seven is more than four.

qa.q: What could Deepak Sir try next to stretch Irfan's counting?
qa.a: He could make two heaps that look similar in size, so Irfan must count rather than just look to find which is more.

qa.q: How might the other children at the anganwadi react to Irfan's shout?
qa.a: They might get curious and want a turn counting and comparing heaps themselves.

grounding: Illustrates a young child counting objects and comparing quantities as more and less, in an anganwadi.

passage: My brother Gautam is five and counts everything now. Yesterday he counted the stairs to our flat: 'Twenty-two!' At tea, Amma gave us grapes. Gautam lined his up and then mine. 'Kunal Bhaiya has more,' he said, pointing at my longer row. I only had one more, but he counted anyway, twice. Amma gave him one extra. He counted again, nodded, and ate them one by one.

qa.q: How many stairs did Gautam count?
qa.a: He counted twenty-two stairs.

qa.q: What does Gautam counting twice suggest he was feeling about the grapes?
qa.a: He seemed anxious that he might be getting less than his brother, so he counted twice to be sure before complaining.

qa.q: How could Amma use grape time to help Gautam learn more about numbers?
qa.a: She could ask him how many more he needs to be equal, turning snack time into a small counting game.

qa.q: How does Kunal see his little brother's counting?
qa.a: Kunal seems a little amused but interested, noticing how carefully Gautam now counts and compares.

grounding: Shows a young child counting and comparing quantities, described by his older brother.

passage: In a small Istanbul park, Zeynep found a big cardboard box by the bins. 'It's a boat!' she told Xin, climbing in and rowing with a stick. Then she tipped it on its side. 'Now it's a tunnel.' Xin crawled through. Zeynep tore off a flap and put it on her head. 'I'm a queen with a paper crown.' Xin tapped the box. 'And this can be our drum.' They banged it until it sagged.

qa.q: Where did Zeynep find the box?
qa.a: She found it by the bins in a small Istanbul park.

qa.q: What does Zeynep's quick switching of ideas suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed excited and full of energy, enjoying finding new uses for the same box.

qa.q: How could a parent support this kind of play?
qa.a: They could let the children keep the box a while and ask 'What else could it be?' without deciding for them.

qa.q: How does Xin add to the game?
qa.a: Xin joins each idea and then adds a new one, the drum, which shows the play feeding both children's imaginations.

grounding: Illustrates children inventing many uses for an everyday object in play, set in Turkey.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Pooja was bored. The queue was long. Lalremsiami, her mother, handed her an empty paper cup from the water cooler. Pooja held it to her ear. 'Hello, Nani?' Then she put it on her finger. 'This is a tiny hat.' She turned it upside down on the chair. 'A cake! Happy birthday, Mumma.' A boy nearby watched, so she made it a trumpet and tooted.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami hand Pooja?
qa.a: She handed her an empty paper cup from the water cooler.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling at the start, and how did it change?
qa.a: She started bored by the long queue, then became playful and absorbed as she invented new uses for the cup.

qa.q: Why was giving Pooja a plain cup a clever idea?
qa.a: A simple object leaves room for imagination, so Pooja could turn it into a phone, hat, cake and trumpet.

qa.q: What might the boy nearby be thinking as he watches?
qa.a: He may be curious and amused, and perhaps wish he could join her game. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young child generating imaginative uses for an everyday object in a clinic waiting room.

passage:
Coach's note, Saturday sports hour, Lokesh Sir
Pema did well on the balance beam today, arms out, eyes on the far end. In 'traffic lights' she stopped when a slower child was in front of her instead of pushing through. When the group was making a circle, she asked her neighbour, 'Can I hold your hand?' and waited for a nod. I pointed this out to the group. 👍

qa.q: What did Pema do when a slower child was in front of her?
qa.a: She stopped instead of pushing through.

qa.q: What does Pema waiting for a nod suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she understood that her neighbour's hand and body belong to them, so she wanted permission first.

qa.q: How could Lokesh Sir help the other children learn from Pema?
qa.a: He could make asking before touching part of every circle game, praising children when they do it.

qa.q: How might the neighbour feel being asked before their hand is held?
qa.a: They would likely feel respected and comfortable, since they got a choice.

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping balance, managing personal space and respecting peers' bodily boundaries.

passage: After the rice harvest, the children raced along the narrow mud bunds between fields. Baljeet ran with arms out like wings, wobbling but never falling in. When Kunal tripped ahead of her, she slowed and leaned sideways so she wouldn't bump him. Later, playing train, Kunal said, 'Don't pull my shirt, it hurts.' Baljeet let go and held his shoulders lightly instead. 'Choo-choo,' she said.

qa.q: Where did the children race after the harvest?
qa.a: They raced along the narrow mud bunds between fields.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet let go of Kunal's shirt?
qa.a: She understood he did not like it and cared that she was hurting him, so she changed how she held on.

qa.q: What could an older cousin do to support this kind of play?
qa.a: They could praise Baljeet for listening and remind all children to check before grabbing each other in games.

qa.q: What would change if Baljeet had ignored Kunal's words?
qa.a: Kunal might feel hurt and not want to play, and the game could turn into a fight.

grounding: Shows a child balancing in active play and respecting a peer's body when asked, in a rural setting.

passage:
"Ammi, look! No hands on the seat!"
"Jaya! You're riding by yourself!" Parveen called.
Jaya wobbled, then pedalled to the gate and back. She hopped off and stood very straight, chin up.
"Did you see? All the way!"
"All the way. How does it feel?"
"Big!" Jaya patted the bike. "Tomorrow I'll show Abbu."
"He'll be so happy."
"I did it myself, na?"

qa.q: How far did Jaya ride on her own?
qa.a: She pedalled to the gate and back.

qa.q: What does Jaya standing very straight with her chin up suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and satisfied after managing to ride by herself.

qa.q: Which part of Parveen's response helped Jaya's pride grow?
qa.a: She asked Jaya how it felt, letting her name her own good feeling instead of only praising her.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when Jaya shows him tomorrow?
qa.a: He would probably feel happy and proud to see her new skill. 🎉

grounding: Illustrates a young child feeling satisfaction and standing taller after an achievement.

passage:
Teacher's note, Anjali Ma'am, UKG
Today Lalremsiami wrote her full name on her worksheet without looking at the name card. It is a long name! She held up the page and stood tall, cheeks pink, and walked around showing it to everyone. 😊 Later she offered to help a friend with her letters. I have pinned the page on the wall.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami write without looking at the name card?
qa.a: She wrote her full name on her worksheet.

qa.q: How can you tell Lalremsiami felt proud?
qa.a: She stood tall with pink cheeks and walked around showing her page to everyone.

qa.q: Why was pinning the page on the wall a good choice?
qa.a: It honours her effort and keeps the achievement visible, which can encourage her to keep trying.

qa.q: How might the friend she helped see Lalremsiami after this?
qa.a: The friend may look up to her and feel encouraged to learn her own letters.

grounding: Shows a child's pride and taller posture after writing her long name, in a teacher's note.

passage: At the school's annual day in Kolkata, Farhan froze on stage. The poem was gone from his head. The hall went quiet. He ran off, crying, and hid behind the curtain. When Reena Ma'am found him, he whispered, 'I'm a bad boy. Everyone saw.' She knelt. 'You forgot some words. That can happen to anyone.' He kept his face buried in his knees, shaking his head.

qa.q: Where did Farhan hide after running off the stage?
qa.a: He hid behind the curtain.

qa.q: What does Farhan saying 'I'm a bad boy' suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt deeply ashamed of his whole self, not just of forgetting, because he had failed in front of everyone.

qa.q: How could Reena Ma'am help Farhan after this moment?
qa.a: She could stay beside him quietly, then later practise the poem with him privately, showing that forgetting did not make him bad.

qa.q: How might Farhan's parents in the audience feel?
qa.a: They might feel worried and sad for him, and want to comfort him rather than scold him.

grounding: Illustrates a young child feeling fundamentally bad about himself after failing in front of others.

passage:
"Oh no, the milk!" Zainab stared at the white puddle.
"It's okay, beta," said Kishore Nana. "I'll get a cloth."
"I'm stupid. I always spill."
"Who said you're stupid?"
"Everyone." She pulled her dupatta over her face.
"The glass was too full. That's all."
"But you wanted me to be careful."
"I still love you. Come, you wipe this side, I'll wipe that one."

qa.q: What did Kishore Nana go to get?
qa.a: He went to get a cloth.

qa.q: Why did Zainab pull her dupatta over her face?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and wanted to hide, believing she was a bad or stupid person because she failed to be careful.

qa.q: What did Kishore Nana say or do that could ease her shame?
qa.a: He blamed the full glass instead of her, reassured her he still loved her, and gave her a way to help fix it.

qa.q: If you were Kishore Nana, what would you want Zainab to understand?
qa.a: That spilling milk is just a small accident and does not make her a bad or stupid child.

grounding: Shows a young child's shame at failing to meet expectations and an elder's gentle response.

passage:
"Francis Bhaiya, your car..." Suraj held out the red car. One wheel was missing.
"What happened?"
"I made it jump off the table. It broke." Suraj's voice shook.
"You broke my car?"
"I'm sorry. I did it." Tears ran down. "I found the wheel. Here."
"Hmm." Francis took it. "Maybe Papa can stick it."
"Can I give you my bus till then?"

qa.q: How did the car break?
qa.a: Suraj made it jump off the table, and a wheel came off.

qa.q: How can you tell Suraj felt guilty about the car?
qa.a: His voice shook and he cried as he admitted 'I did it', and he tried to make up for it.

qa.q: What went right in how Suraj handled his mistake?
qa.a: He owned up to the specific wrong, brought back the wheel and offered his bus, which are ways to repair harm.

qa.q: How might Francis feel after hearing Suraj's apology?
qa.a: He may still be annoyed about his car, but softened by Suraj's honesty and offer.

grounding: Illustrates a young child recognising a specific wrong he did and feeling remorse for it.

passage:
Teacher's note, Parveen Ma'am, Class 1
Today Nazia tore a classmate's drawing when she didn't get the green crayon. The classmate cried. Ten minutes later, Nazia came to me, eyes wet: 'I tore it. I shouldn't have.' She asked for tape and fixed it with her friend, very carefully. I thanked her for telling me. We will talk about waiting for crayons tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Nazia tear the drawing?
qa.a: She tore it when she didn't get the green crayon.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she came to the teacher with wet eyes?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sorry for what she had done, and wanted to own up to it.

qa.q: What could Parveen Ma'am teach about waiting for crayons?
qa.a: She could practise simple ways to wait, like asking 'Can I have it next?', so anger does not turn into tearing.

qa.q: How might the classmate feel when Nazia helps tape the drawing?
qa.a: The classmate may feel cared for and less hurt, seeing that Nazia is truly sorry. 🙂

grounding: Shows a child recognising her specific wrong action and feeling remorse, in a teacher's note.

passage:
Note by Nandini Ma'am, LKG
It was Keerthana's birthday today. When the whole class stood and sang loudly to her, she covered her face with both hands and slid under her desk. Her ears went red. I lowered my voice and asked the class to sing softly. She peeped out at the end. Later, one-on-one, she happily told me about her cake. 🎂

qa.q: Where did Keerthana go when the class sang?
qa.a: She slid under her desk.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana have covered her face?
qa.a: The sudden loud attention from the whole class may have felt too much, making her feel shy and exposed.

qa.q: Which choice by Nandini Ma'am helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking the class to sing softly reduced the attention so Keerthana could feel safe enough to peep out.

qa.q: How might the classmates see Keerthana hiding?
qa.a: Some may be puzzled, since they meant to be kind, and might not know that big attention can feel uncomfortable.

grounding: Illustrates a young child's sudden self-consciousness at overwhelming attention, in a teacher's note.

passage: At her cousin's wedding in the village, the dhol started and Leela, five, danced in her new lehenga. Suddenly all the aunties formed a circle, clapping and calling, 'Look at Leela!' Someone held up a phone. Leela stopped mid-spin. Her face crumpled, and she ran to her aunt Gurleen, burying her face in her saree. 'Too many people,' she mumbled. Gurleen led her to the quiet steps.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen lead Leela?
qa.a: She led her to the quiet steps.

qa.q: What made Leela stop dancing mid-spin, and how did she feel?
qa.a: Everyone suddenly watching and filming her made her feel embarrassed and overwhelmed.

qa.q: How could the adults at the wedding support Leela next time?
qa.a: They could cheer from where they are without crowding her or filming, and let her dance when she is ready.

qa.q: How might the aunties see Leela running away?
qa.a: They may be surprised, since they meant their praise kindly, and not realise it felt like too much.

grounding: Shows a young child's sudden embarrassment at unwanted attention during a village wedding.

passage:
Playground note by Wasim Sir
During break, a Class 1 girl fell off the slide and cried loudly. Hrithik, who was playing tag, stopped running. His face fell, and he stood very still, watching her. Then he came to me: 'Sir, she's hurt. She's crying a lot.' He stayed near until her knee was cleaned, not going back to his game. I told him it was kind to tell me.

qa.q: What was Hrithik doing before the girl fell?
qa.a: He was playing tag.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's face falling and standing still suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt sad and worried for the girl when he saw her cry.

qa.q: How could Wasim Sir build on Hrithik's concern?
qa.a: He could talk with Hrithik about what else helps when someone is hurt, like asking if they are okay.

qa.q: How might the hurt girl feel if she learned Hrithik got help?
qa.a: She might feel cared for by someone she barely knew, and less alone.

grounding: Illustrates a young child feeling sorrow and concern on seeing another's distress.

passage: In the potter's yard at the edge of the village, Leela's clay pot cracked in the kiln. She sat on the ground and sobbed. Naveen, five, had been chasing a hen, but he stopped. He watched her tears, his lip turning down. Slowly he came and sat beside her, not saying anything. After a while he said, 'Your pot was nice,' and touched the broken piece gently.

qa.q: What happened to Leela's clay pot?
qa.a: It cracked in the kiln.

qa.q: How can you tell Naveen felt sad for Leela?
qa.a: He stopped chasing the hen, his lip turned down as he watched her tears, and he came to sit beside her.

qa.q: What could an adult nearby do to support both children?
qa.a: They could comfort Leela and quietly tell Naveen that sitting with her was a caring thing to do.

qa.q: What is it like for Leela to have Naveen sit with her?
qa.a: It may make her feel less alone in her sadness, even though her pot is still broken.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling sorrow and concern upon seeing another child's distress, in a village.

passage:
Daycare note by Chetan Sir
Today a boy caught his finger in the cupboard door and howled. Kashish, who had been building, ran over. She patted his back fast and said, 'Don't cry, don't cry.' Then she fetched her own blanket, the one she never shares, and put it on his lap. I cleaned his finger. Kashish sat close, stroking his hair until he calmed.

qa.q: What did Kashish fetch for the hurt boy?
qa.a: She fetched her own blanket, the one she never shares.

qa.q: What does Kashish giving her special blanket suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she really wanted him to feel better and was moved enough by his pain to give up something she values.

qa.q: How could Chetan Sir help Kashish grow her comforting skills?
qa.a: He could thank her and suggest other things that help, like asking the hurt person what they need.

qa.q: How might the boy remember Kashish after this?
qa.a: He might see her as a kind friend and feel closer to her. ❤️

grounding: Illustrates a young child noticing another's pain and offering simple comfort, in a daycare note.

passage: Dadi winced and rubbed her back as she got up from the courtyard floor. Eshaan, sorting marbles, looked up. 'Dadi, ouch?' Alka Dadi nodded. He ran to fetch her flat pillow from the charpai and pushed it behind her. Then he brought her steel tumbler of water, spilling a bit. 'Drink.' He patted her hand like she pats his when he falls.

qa.q: What did Eshaan bring Dadi after the pillow?
qa.a: He brought her steel tumbler of water.

qa.q: What made Eshaan leave his marbles, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: He noticed Dadi was in pain and felt worried for her, wanting to help her feel better.

qa.q: How could Alka Dadi respond to encourage Eshaan's care?
qa.a: She could thank him warmly and tell him the pillow helped, so he knows his comfort matters.

qa.q: What does Eshaan patting her hand show about where he learned comforting?
qa.a: It shows he copies the care Dadi gives him when he falls, now turning it back to her.

grounding: Shows a young child noticing a grandparent's pain and trying simple comfort, in a rural home.

passage: In the lane outside the kirana shop, Ojas lost his last marble to Chetan. His lip pushed out and his fists clenched. 'Not fair!' He kicked the dust once. Chetan shrugged and held up the marble. Ojas turned away, breathing hard, and stared at the buffalo tied nearby. After a moment he turned back. 'Play again? I'll win this time.' Chetan grinned and set the marbles down.

qa.q: Where were the boys playing marbles?
qa.a: They were playing in the lane outside the kirana shop.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he kicked the dust?
qa.a: He was angry and disappointed at losing his last marble.

qa.q: What helped Ojas recover without a long meltdown?
qa.a: Turning away and looking at the buffalo gave him a short break to breathe, so he could calm down and try again.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Ojas coming back to play?
qa.a: He would likely be glad the game can go on, rather than having to deal with a long sulk.

grounding: Illustrates a child recovering from a lost game after brief frustration, in a small-town lane.

passage: At the kitchen table in Valencia, Dalia's counter slid down the longest snake, all the way back to the start. 'Noooo!' She threw her dice on the floor and crossed her arms. Santiago, her big brother, waited. Dalia huffed and stared at the ceiling. Then she climbed off her chair, picked up the dice and plonked it back. 'Fine. I'm still playing.' Two turns later, she hit a ladder and cheered.

qa.q: Where did Dalia's counter slide back to?
qa.a: It slid all the way back to the start.

qa.q: What was Dalia feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and cross about losing her progress in the game.

qa.q: What did Santiago's waiting give Dalia?
qa.a: It gave her space to calm down on her own instead of being scolded or rushed.

qa.q: What would change if Santiago had teased her for throwing the dice?
qa.a: She might have grown angrier and stopped playing, turning a short upset into a longer meltdown.

grounding: Shows a young child bouncing back from a setback in a game without a prolonged meltdown, in Spain.
